title: House and Bell
premise: Orsen Fairweather hosts a small-town overnight radio show, but lately the callers are people who died the week before, and their requests grow stranger: count the doors, keep the lights on, don't answer the second voice. When Orsen's sleep recordings reveal a presence answering questions in a borrowed cadence, they realize the house they broadcast from was once home to Judge Aldous Wren, who hanged himself rather than sign away the town to a creditor with no face. The entity now circling the station is that creditor's collector, and it needs one living signature—Orsen's—to finish what the judge refused. Holding out until sunrise, Orsen rallies the dead callers and the found family of insomniac listeners into a chorus of refusal, and at dawn signs nothing, instead reading the judge's suppressed verdict on air, breaking the contract's power and freeing both the house and the dead.
about_author: A. M. Coldharbour is the pen name of a former night-shift dispatcher who claims to have taken calls from three towns that don't appear on maps. They write exclusively between midnight and dawn, and refuse to discuss the fourth town.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A routine overnight broadcast takes its first wrong turn when a caller describes her own funeral from last Tuesday. Orsen keeps talking, professional to the last, but locks the studio door after she hangs up. Emotional beat: denial dressed as professionalism.

chapters.title: The Door Count
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A second caller, a drowned man, asks Orsen to count the doors of the station aloud on air. There are eleven. There were ten yesterday. Orsen complies, telling themselves it's good radio. Beat: unease curdling into complicity.

chapters.title: Listener Mail
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Letters arrive postmarked after their senders' deaths, all asking variations of 'is it awake yet?' Orsen tapes them inside a desk drawer like evidence. Beat: the first admission, private and trembling, that something real is happening.

chapters.title: Sleep Study
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Reviewing their own sleep-recording app for an insomnia segment, Orsen hears a second voice answering questions they never asked aloud. It knows their mother's maiden name. Beat: violation; the self is no longer private territory.

chapters.title: The Regulars
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV rotating through three night-owl listeners: a trucker, a hospice nurse, a teenage insomniac named Pip. Each has noticed the dead calling in. They begin comparing notes in the chat room. Beat: fragile solidarity forming in the dark.

chapters.title: House History
chapters.summary: Pip's POV. Pip digs into the station building's past: it was Judge Aldous Wren's home until his suicide in 1961, the night before he was to sign over the town's water rights. Beat: curiosity sharpening into dread.

chapters.title: Second Voice
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. On air, the second voice answers a caller directly, using Orsen's mouth for half a sentence. Orsen plays it off as a technical glitch while gripping the desk. Beat: terror masked by performance.

chapters.title: The Creditor
chapters.summary: Judge Wren's diary excerpts, read by Orsen on air, describe a visitor with no face who offered relief from every debt—for one signature. The diary stops mid-sentence. Beat: the horror acquires a shape and a purpose.

chapters.title: Lights On
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Every bulb in the building burns out except the studio. The dead callers explain: light is testimony; darkness is where signatures happen. Orsen rigs work lights and stays put. Beat: grim resolve.

chapters.title: Pip Comes Over
chapters.summary: Pip's POV. Against all advice, Pip bikes to the station at 2 a.m., needing to see it. Orsen lets them in, furious and relieved. Eleven doors; they count twelve. Beat: found family's first risky step toward each other.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Reconstructing the night of Wren's death, Orsen realizes the judge invited the collector in for tea—a courtesy that became consent. Hospitality is the loophole. Beat: horrified understanding of the trap's mechanics.

chapters.title: The Hospice Nurse
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol recognizes the second voice: it spoke through a dying patient of hers, coaxing her to co-sign paperwork. She drives to the station with her own recordings. Beat: allies converging, evidence accumulating.

chapters.title: Trucker's Toll
chapters.summary: Dell's POV. Dell recounts a rest-stop encounter with a polite man who had no reflection and asked him to witness a document. Dell refused; his rig's engine died until sunrise. Beat: the pattern confirmed across strangers.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The FCC threatens to shut the station down after complaints about 'the dead woman on channel nine.' Losing the transmitter means losing the dead's only doorway. Beat: external pressure tightening around the supernatural siege.

chapters.title: The Twelfth Door
chapters.summary: Pip and Orsen's shared POV. Behind the twelfth door: Wren's sealed study, untouched since 1961, smelling of ink and rain. On the desk, a contract with one blank line. Beat: awe curdling to revulsion.

chapters.title: Blank Line
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The contract bears every resident's name since Wren—except his. He never signed. The collector has waited sixty years for someone with authority over the house. Orsen is the current resident. Beat: the personal stakes crystallize.

chapters.title: Sunrise Deadline
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The dead callers confirm it: the offer expires at dawn. If no one signs by then, the collector must leave—but it can take the house's living residents with it. Beat: hope and threat arriving together.

chapters.title: Power Outage
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The grid fails. Backup generator holds the studio lights only. In the dark wings of the house, footsteps practice Orsen's walk. Beat: siege begins; isolation within the found family's gathering place.

chapters.title: Mimic
chapters.summary: Pip's POV. Something wearing Orsen's voice calls Pip from the studio hallway, asking them to open door eleven. Pip nearly does, saved by a detail only the real Orsen would know—the show's opening line. Beat: trust tested and barely holding.

chapters.title: The Dead Organize
chapters.summary: Ensemble of dead callers' POVs, brief and overlapping. The deceased listeners compare notes among themselves: the collector feeds on consent, starves on refusal. They begin planning how to testify. Beat: the dead become protagonists.

chapters.title: Wren's Verdict
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. In the study, Orsen finds the judgment Wren wrote instead of signing: a legal finding that the creditor's claim was void ab initio, never filed because filing required the signature. Justice drafted, never delivered. Beat: revelation of the weapon hidden in plain sight.

chapters.title: First Assault
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The collector stops pretending. Doors slam in sequence, the temperature drops, and the second voice reads Orsen's debts aloud—every lie told on air, every person let down. Beat: shame weaponized; Orsen wavers.

chapters.title: Confession Broadcast
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV live on air. Instead of signing, Orsen confesses their failures to the listening dead and living alike. The lights steady. Testimony, it turns out, is also consent—to truth. Beat: vulnerability as armor; turning point.

chapters.title: Pip's Bargain
chapters.summary: Pip's POV. The collector offers Pip what it offered everyone: erase your grief, bring back your dead brother—one signature. Pip says no, crying, shaking, saying no. Beat: the youngest member passes the test the judge failed.

chapters.title: Marisol's Records
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Her deathbed recordings, played on air, catch the collector's true name in a patient's last breath. Names bind. The studio lights flare white. Beat: the hunt flips; the hunters become the hunted.

chapters.title: Dell Blocks the Road
chapters.summary: Dell's POV. The collector tries to leave the property to reset the deadline. Dell parks his rig across the only exit, engine running, headlights blazing, refusing to move. Beat: ordinary courage as a wall.

chapters.title: Eleven Doors, Sealed
chapters.summary: Orsen and Pip's alternating POV. Following the dead's instructions, they chalk the judge's verdict text across each threshold. Ten doors seal. The twelfth won't take the chalk—it drinks it. Beat: preparation, dread, one door left open.

chapters.title: The Collector Speaks
chapters.summary: Collector's POV, cold and reasonable. It explains it isn't evil; it is enforcement. Contracts exist because people sign them. It offers Orsen the same deal it offered Wren, sweetened: everyone Orsen loves, safe forever. Beat: temptation at its most articulate.

chapters.title: Found Family Vote
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. In the studio, the living—Orsen, Pip, Marisol, Dell—vote on what to do. Unanimous: no signature, ever, even for safety. The dead listeners call in to add their voices. Beat: found family becomes a deliberative body; warmth inside horror.

chapters.title: Blackout Hour
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The generator dies. Total dark, total silence except breathing. The collector moves through the house unbound, whispering signatures into sleeping ears. Orsen recites the verdict from memory to keep the light of it alive. Beat: darkest hour; endurance without resources.

chapters.title: What Wren Saw
chapters.summary: Judge Wren's ghost POV, the first and only time. He lingers in the study, ashamed for sixty years, watching Orsen hold the line he couldn't. He begins, slowly, to speak. Beat: redemption stirring in the story's original failure.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Dawn is forty minutes out. The collector produces fresh papers: if the current resident signs, everything ends cleanly. If not, it will drag the house—and everyone in it—into whatever holds the unsigned. Beat: ultimatum; clock audibly ticking.

chapters.title: Testimony of the Dead
chapters.summary: Ensemble dead-callers' POV. One by one, the dead flood the phone lines, each giving witness to what the collector took from them—not signatures, but the small consents of despair. The switchboard glows. Beat: chorus of the wronged; rising crescendo.

chapters.title: Wren Signs Nothing
chapters.summary: Wren's ghost POV. The judge manifests in the studio, takes the pen, and before the whole assembled dark, formally refuses again—this time witnessed, this time recorded. His refusal, spoken aloud, completes the verdict he wrote. Beat: catharsis; the old wound answered.

chapters.title: Reading the Verdict
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen reads Wren's full judgment on air: the claim void, the debt imaginary, the contract null. The words act like sunlight. Doors slam shut one final time—all eleven, then the twelfth seals itself. Beat: climax; language as exorcism.

chapters.title: The Collector Withdraws
chapters.summary: Collector's POV, fraying. Bound by its own rules, it must honor a properly entered void judgment. It gathers its papers and pours itself out through the chimney like smoke remembering being fire. Beat: the monster defeated not by force but by procedure and nerve.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Dawn floods the studio. The dead callers say goodbye one at a time, grateful, going quiet mid-sentence like candles pinched out gently. Orsen stays on air until the last one hangs up. Beat: grief and peace braided together.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Days later: the FCC investigation dissolves, the town's water rights quietly revert, and the four survivors keep meeting for breakfast though the show could end. Beat: the found family persists beyond crisis.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Final broadcast. Orsen retires the show, counts the doors one last time—ten, always ten now—and thanks the listeners, living and otherwise. Beat: closure; gratitude without sentimentality.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Pip's POV, epilogue. Pip visits the study, now a small museum of Wren's life. On the desk, the contract has faded to blank paper. Pip leaves a note: 'We kept the lights on.' Somewhere, faintly, a bell rings once. Beat: quiet wonder; the house at rest, the story resonating.
